introduction.p: A cyclist riding at {20\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut ft}{\rm\mathstrut s}}} rides past a dog. A moment later, when the bicycle is {40\ {\rm ft}} away, the dog begins to chase the bicycle at a speed of {30\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut ft}{\rm\mathstrut s}}}\text{.} Assuming the cyclist does not change course or speed, how long will it be until the dog catches up to the bicycle?

statement.p: Write two equations that form a system for this scenario.

solution.p: The bicycle starts out {40\ {\rm ft}} away and is traveling at {20\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut ft}{\rm\mathstrut s}}}\text{.} So one equation is {d = 20t+40}\text{.}
The dog starts running at time t=0 with speed {30\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut ft}{\rm\mathstrut s}}}\text{.} So the other equation is {d = 30t}\text{.}

statement.p: Plot the lines for the system of two equations.

image.shortdescription: a Cartesian grid with two intersecting lines; one line passes through (0,40) with slope 20; the other line passes through (0,0) with slope 30; the lines cross at (4,120)

statement.p: Based on the graph, how long will it be until the dog catches up with the bicycle?
How far will that be from the place where the dog started running?

solution.p: The lines cross at (4,120)\text{.} So after 4 seconds, the cyclist and the dog are each 120 feet away from where the dog started running.
